newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE Euroyen futures down on machinery orders.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE Euroyen futures down on machinery orders.

text.p: The key September three-month Euroyen futures contract ended Tuesday's TIFFE day session lower in reaction to a jump in Japan's machinery orders.
Private-sector machinery orders, excluding those for machinery at electric power firms and for ships, rose a seasonally adjusted 44.2 percent in October.
The September contract closed down 0.02 at 99.17, after trading between 99.20 and 99.16.
Trading volume for the September contract was 65,339.
"Euroyen futures fell after the release of machinery orders. People are now worried how November orders would turn out," said a city bank trader.

An Economic Planning Agency official told reporters that November machinery orders were likely to show a drop after a strong October figure. But he added that if November orders fell less than 10 percent, the EPA could say private-sector orders were on a rising trend.
"Bargain-hunting interest emerged after the September fell to its intraday low," a trader at another city bank said.
"The market opened firmer following an overnight rise in U.S. stocks and bonds. However, the September failed to break above 99.20. It looks toppish at that level for now," said the first trader.
Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita's remarks were largely dismissed by the market, as it provided no fresh insights about the economy, traders said.

Matsushita told a parliamentary budget committee meeting that Japan's economy was continuing a gradual recovery and the strength of the recovery was becoming firmer, but added firms were taking a cautious stance towards economic prospects.
In the interbank money market, the key unsecured overnight call money was traded at 0.49 percent, down from 0.50 percent on Monday.
The BOJ injected a net 200 billion yen into the money market in the morning, maintaining a neutral stance.
"The overnight rate was slightly softer because fund demand related to the public sector's bonus payment has eased," said a trader at a regional bank.
Three-month certificates of deposit (CDs) were issued at 0.51 and 0.50 percent.
